Investors will now weigh expected scale and pipeline access against integration risk, commodity-price exposure and the possibility that transaction terms or timing change before closing.
dek: The all-stock transaction would create the largest publicly traded producer focused on Alberta’s Clearwater Formation.
headline: Tamarack and Headwater agree to $7.25 billion oil merger

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Verizon signed a multibillion-dollar agreement with Corning for high-density optical fiber and connectivity products, extending a supplier relationship that has lasted about three decades.

Reuters reported that Corning will provide more than 80 million miles of fiber between 2027 and 2032. Verizon said the equipment will support broadband expansion for homes and businesses and add capacity for large AI computing customers that need fast, low-latency connections.

The companies described the agreement as multibillion-dollar but did not disclose exact financial terms. That limits how precisely investors can estimate revenue timing, margins or capital requirements from the announcement alone.

The deal illustrates how AI spending is expanding beyond processors and data centers into the networks connecting them. For Corning, it provides a long-duration customer commitment; for Verizon, it secures supply for planned construction. The ultimate financial effect will depend on deployment pace, customer demand and execution over several years. No stock price in this report should be treated as a live quote.
dek: Corning will supply more than 80 million miles of high-density optical fiber from 2027 through 2032 for broadband and AI infrastructure.
headline: Verizon signs multibillion-dollar fiber deal with Corning

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The Boston Bruins signed center Fraser Minten to a seven-year, $50.4 million contract extension Tuesday, locking up the 22-year-old through the 2033-34 season.

The Associated Press reported that the deal carries an average annual value and salary-cap hit of $7.2 million. Minten will first complete the final year of his rookie contract, which pays a base salary of $850,000 this season.

Boston acquired Minten from Toronto in March 2025 in the trade that sent defenseman Brandon Carlo to the Maple Leafs. Minten then played all 82 games last season, recording career highs of 17 goals and 18 assists. His 35 points were the most by a Bruins rookie since 2017-18, and his plus-21 rating led NHL rookies.

The extension gives Boston a younger long-term piece alongside established stars David Pastrnak and Charlie McAvoy. It also shifts performance risk to the club: the contract becomes especially valuable if Minten continues developing, but costly if his production stalls. The announced value is the full contract total, not a one-season salary.
dek: The 22-year-old center is under contract through 2033-34 after producing 35 points in his first full season with Boston.
headline: Bruins sign Fraser Minten to seven-year, $50.4 million extension

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Yolanda Celucci, a longtime Boston fashion designer and philanthropist known across the region’s style and charitable communities, has died at age 91.

WHDH reported that Celucci worked with celebrities, designers and presidents during a career that made her a prominent figure in Boston fashion. She also used that visibility to support charitable fundraising.

Through the Waltham Lions Club, Celucci helped raise millions of dollars for charity, according to the station. That work connected her fashion career with causes serving people in Greater Boston and beyond.

The report did not state a cause of death or provide funeral arrangements. Celucci is survived by a daughter, grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Her legacy rests in both the public events and designs that shaped Boston’s fashion scene and the fundraising relationships she built over decades. Additional details about memorial services may be released by her family or community organizations. Her death closes a notable chapter in the region’s creative and civic life.
dek: A prominent figure in the region’s fashion community, Celucci also helped raise millions of dollars for charity through the Waltham Lions Club.
headline: Boston fashion designer and philanthropist Yolanda Celucci dies at 91

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: New Hampshire primary voters describe distrust and ambivalence
dek: Interviews at polling places found many Granite Staters voting from civic duty or concern about specific issues rather than enthusiasm for candidates.
body: New Hampshire voters who spoke with NHPR at polling places Tuesday repeatedly described distrust, frustration or ambivalence toward candidates, even as they cast ballots in the state primary.

The interviews were not a scientific survey and should not be read as a statewide measure. They nevertheless captured a recurring mood across several communities: some voters said civic duty brought them out, while others were motivated by particular issues or by the November general election rather than strong attachment to a primary candidate.

Education funding and property taxes were among the concerns voters raised. Others focused on federal gridlock, campaign funding and immigration enforcement. Several town moderators told NHPR that turnout is often lighter in nonpresidential primaries.

The reporting adds context to the results already being called Tuesday night. Winners will move on to November, but the comments suggest nominees will also have to persuade voters who entered the fall campaign skeptical of political institutions and unconvinced that candidates will deliver change. The anecdotes show individual views, not a definitive picture of the electorate.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Mount Washington tribute will shine twin beams for four nights
dek: The Honor Summit remembrance begins Wednesday, with organizers shortening nightly hours after consulting wildlife specialists.
body: Two beams of light are scheduled to rise from the summit of Mount Washington on four nights this week as part of the Honor Summit remembrance of the September 11 attacks.

The Conway Daily Sun reported that Gov. Kelly Ayotte is expected in Conway Wednesday for the kickoff. Organizers say the installation will honor those killed in the attacks, first responders and veterans. The beams are scheduled to operate September 9 through 12 from 8 p.m. to midnight.

Producers shortened the original seven-hour nightly plan after discussions with New Hampshire Fish and Game, New Hampshire Audubon and the Cornell Lab of Ornithology about fall bird migration. An Audubon representative is expected to monitor the area, and organizers said the lights can be interrupted if large flocks are observed.

The event has obtained permits from the Federal Aviation Administration and state wildlife officials, according to the newspaper. Organizers also plan to direct money raised beyond expenses to four veterans-service nonprofits. The four-night schedule balances the public memorial with efforts to reduce effects on wildlife around the 6,288-foot summit.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Chicopee electric dirt-bike rider faces charges after crash
dek: Police say the unregistered and uninsured bike had no headlight or taillight when it collided with a vehicle near an I-391 offramp.
body: A 28-year-old man is facing criminal charges after the electric dirt bike he was riding collided with a vehicle in Chicopee, police said Tuesday.

Western Mass News reported that emergency crews were called to Chicopee Street at about 10:15 p.m. Friday. Investigators said the dirt bike struck a vehicle that was leaving the Interstate 391 offramp and turning left onto Chicopee Street.

Police said the dirt bike had no headlight or taillight and was not registered or insured for public-road use. The rider was injured and taken to a hospital; the driver of the other vehicle was not hurt. Authorities did not publicly detail the rider’s condition.

The case is one of several recent western Massachusetts incidents involving off-road vehicles used on streets. Police emphasized that electric dirt bikes and similar vehicles must meet applicable registration, insurance and equipment rules when operated on public roads. The allegations have not been proven in court, and the report did not identify the rider or list a court date.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Police say Jeep fled Chicopee stop before striking Agawam ambulance
dek: A new police account links the weekend Springfield crash to an earlier traffic stop; two paramedics suffered minor injuries.
body: Chicopee police said Tuesday that a Jeep involved in a weekend crash with an Agawam ambulance had fled an attempted traffic stop earlier that night.

Western Mass News reported that the ambulance was traveling on a mutual-aid call when the vehicles collided around 1:30 a.m. Saturday at Boland Way and East Columbus Avenue in Springfield. Two Agawam firefighter-paramedics were treated for minor injuries.

A passenger in the Jeep was ejected and taken to a hospital. Police said there were no reported serious injuries from the crash, though the passenger’s specific condition was not released. The Jeep’s driver, a Palmer man, was detained by Springfield police and transferred to Chicopee police.

Authorities said the driver faces multiple charges, but the station’s update did not provide the complete list or identify him. The allegations have not been proven in court. The new account clarifies the sequence before the collision while leaving questions about speed, impairment and the final crash reconstruction unanswered. The ambulance had been in service for less than a month.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Peach Cobbler Factory opens first New England shop in Providence
dek: The Southern-dessert chain has opened near Federal Hill with cobblers, banana pudding, cinnamon rolls and late-night weekend hours.
body: The Peach Cobbler Factory has opened its first New England location at 102 Dean Street in Providence, bringing the fast-growing Southern-dessert chain to the edge of Federal Hill.

NBC 10 WJAR reported Tuesday that the location is one of more than 120 nationwide. Its menu includes warm cobblers, banana puddings, cinnamon rolls, brownies, cookies, milkshakes and ice cream, with four-item dessert flights for customers who want smaller portions of several selections.

The Providence shop is open from noon to 10 p.m. Sunday through Tuesday, noon to midnight Wednesday and Thursday, and noon to 2:30 a.m. Friday and Saturday, according to the company’s location page. Delivery and catering are also advertised.

The opening adds a nationally known sweets brand to a neighborhood best known for independent restaurants and Italian food. Early customer traffic will show whether social-media recognition translates into repeat local business after the novelty period. The company has not disclosed hiring totals or projected sales for the Providence franchise.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Route 146 wrong-way crash suspect arraigned on DUI charges
dek: Kevin Migna was released on personal recognizance and ordered not to drive after an August crash that injured one person.
body: A man accused of driving the wrong way and causing a crash on Route 146 in Lincoln was arraigned Tuesday on charges that include driving under the influence resulting in serious bodily injury.

NBC 10 WJAR reported that the August 29 collision happened around 9 p.m. near the Breakneck Hill Road exit. Police said a vehicle entered the southbound highway while traveling north, and one person was injured.

Kevin Migna also faces reckless-driving and DUI-of-liquor charges. No plea was entered at the hearing, and he was referred to a public defender. A judge released him on personal recognizance and ordered him not to drive.

A pre-arraignment conference is scheduled for December 7. The charges are allegations, and Migna is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Tuesday’s court appearance moves the case from the initial police investigation into the judicial process, where evidence about the vehicle’s direction, the driver’s condition and the injured person’s medical status can be tested.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Iran launches missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan after tanker strikes
dek: Jordan said it intercepted most of 18 ballistic missiles as the latest U.S.-Iran exchange raised fears of a wider regional conflict.
body: Iran launched ballistic missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan after American forces struck five Iranian oil tankers, according to Iranian state media and reporting by the Associated Press.

Jordan said its forces intercepted most of 18 missiles. The AP reported no immediate American casualties from the launch. The exchange followed U.S. Central Command’s announcement that it destroyed or disabled five tankers after Iranian missile attacks on a U.S. Navy warship.

The latest action expands the immediate geography of the confrontation and increases risks for military personnel, commercial shipping and neighboring countries. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard also warned tankers near Kuwait and Bahrain to leave the area, while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains under pressure.

Information is still developing. Claims from the combatants may change as governments release radar data, damage assessments and casualty reports. The reported missile count and interceptions come from official statements cited by the AP, not an independent NorthEast News assessment. The next verified military response will determine whether the exchange remains limited or draws in additional regional forces.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Hurricane Lowell knocks out power across Kauai and damages coast
dek: Nearly all of the island utility’s members lost electricity as destructive winds, heavy rain and large waves battered western Hawaii.
body: Hurricane Lowell’s outer winds and rain caused widespread damage across Kauai Tuesday, knocking out power to nearly all of the island utility’s roughly 35,000 members and sending hundreds of residents to shelters.

The Associated Press reported that trees fell, coastal infrastructure was damaged and debris washed inland along parts of Kauai’s southern shore. Lihue Airport recorded sustained winds above 50 mph, with gusts reaching 80 mph.

The storm’s center passed west of Hawaii, but its broad circulation still affected several islands. Warnings were lifted Tuesday morning, while authorities continued to caution about flooding, mudslides, blocked roads and lingering high water. Oahu also reported flooded routes.

Recovery conditions remain fluid. Emergency managers asked residents to avoid unnecessary travel while crews assess roads and restore electricity. The power-outage total describes the disruption reported during the storm, not a live restoration figure. Updated utility counts, damage inspections and rainfall measurements will provide a clearer view of the hurricane’s full impact.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: OpenAI expands AI tools into chip design and specialized industries
dek: The company says its models helped move an internal chip project to tape-out in nine months as it pursues enterprise work beyond general chat.
body: OpenAI is expanding its artificial-intelligence services into chip design, life sciences and financial services as it seeks more specialized enterprise work, Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar said Tuesday.

Reuters reported that OpenAI used its own models while developing a chip project called Jalapeno, which reached the tape-out stage in nine months. Tape-out marks the point when a finalized design is sent for manufacturing; it does not mean the chip is already in mass production.

Friar said the company is emphasizing outcome-based tools that can be measured against customer costs and productivity. She also described enterprise revenue as growing faster than overall annualized revenue during the latest reported monthly period.

The chip-design example points to a broader shift from general-purpose assistants toward systems embedded in technical workflows. Performance, security and the cost of checking model output will be central for companies deciding whether to use AI in design work where errors can be expensive. OpenAI did not disclose manufacturing yield, benchmark results or a commercial release date for the chip-design service.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: FCC proposes opening more spectrum for space-based broadband
dek: The agency plans a September 30 vote on changes covering the 12 GHz and 42 GHz bands, satellite links and ultra-wideband devices.
body: The Federal Communications Commission proposed opening additional wireless spectrum for space-based broadband and modernizing several related technology rules, with a commission vote set for September 30.

Reuters reported that the proposal covers more than 1,000 megahertz in the 12 GHz and 42 GHz bands. The agency says the capacity could support high-speed satellite connectivity for homes, aircraft, ships and ground networks, as well as more resilient links between satellites.

The FCC also wants to update rules for ultra-wideband devices used in package tracking, industrial systems, vehicle technology and imaging. Separate permitting changes are intended to speed deployment of internet infrastructure.

The proposal begins a regulatory step, not an immediate spectrum opening. Commissioners must vote, and implementation can still involve technical conditions designed to prevent interference with existing users. Satellite operators, wireless carriers and equipment makers will be watching the final band plan and power rules closely because those details determine which services can operate and how quickly new hardware can reach customers.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Holtec Nuclear seeks up to $10.2 billion valuation in U.S. IPO
dek: The New Jersey company plans to offer 50 million shares as investor interest grows around nuclear power and data-center electricity demand.
body: Holtec Nuclear is seeking a valuation of up to $10.2 billion in a U.S. initial public offering, opening a closely watched fall listing window for energy and infrastructure companies.

Reuters reported that the Camden, New Jersey-based company plans to offer 50 million shares at $15 to $18 each, potentially raising as much as $900 million. Holtec expects to list on Nasdaq and Nasdaq Texas under the ticker HNUC.

The company makes reactor components and spent-fuel storage systems, handles nuclear-plant decommissioning and is developing small modular reactors. It is also working to restart the 800-megawatt Palisades plant in Michigan, an effort that would return a previously decommissioned U.S. commercial reactor to service.

The targeted valuation and proceeds are terms in an offering plan, not a completed sale or live market price. Investor demand can still change the range, timing or final amount raised. The IPO will test how much public-market enthusiasm for rising data-center electricity demand extends to companies with long nuclear-project timelines and substantial regulatory requirements.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: EverBank and WaFd agree to $3.9 billion reverse merger
dek: The all-stock transaction would create a bank with about $75 billion in assets and give EverBank’s investors a majority stake.
body: EverBank Financial and WaFd agreed to a $3.9 billion all-stock reverse merger that would create a publicly traded bank with about $75 billion in assets.

Under the companies’ agreement, EverBank will merge into WaFd at the holding-company level, while WaFd Bank will merge into EverBank’s national-bank charter. The public company would take the EverBank Financial name and trade on Nasdaq under the ticker EVBK.

EverBank investors are expected to own 59.2% of the combined company, with current WaFd shareholders holding 40.8%. The banks project roughly $58 billion in loans and $59 billion in deposits after the transaction. EverBank chief executive Greg Seibly is expected to lead the combined business.

The deal is targeted to close in early 2027, subject to regulatory and WaFd shareholder approvals. The announced $3.9 billion value and projected financial benefits are transaction estimates, not live market prices or guaranteed results. Investors will weigh the larger deposit base and geographic reach against integration costs, credit risk and the possibility that regulators impose conditions.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Patriots rule out TreVeyon Henderson for season opener in Seattle
dek: The running back will miss Wednesday’s Super Bowl rematch because of an ankle injury, increasing the expected workload for Rhamondre Stevenson.
body: The New England Patriots ruled out running back TreVeyon Henderson for Wednesday night’s season opener against the Seattle Seahawks because of an ankle injury.

Reuters reported that Henderson has been dealing with the injury since an August 24 practice. He led New England with 911 rushing yards and nine rushing touchdowns as a rookie last season and also played in the Patriots’ Super Bowl LX loss to Seattle.

Veteran Rhamondre Stevenson is expected to carry a larger share of the backfield work. Offensive lineman Ben Brown was also ruled out with a knee injury, while defensive tackle Christian Barmore has no injury designation for the game.

Seattle listed safety Ty Okada out and safety Nick Emmanwori and wide receiver Tory Horton as questionable. Kickoff is scheduled for 8:20 p.m. Eastern at Lumen Field. The injury designations are the teams’ official pregame status reports and can still be supplemented by inactive lists released closer to kickoff. Henderson’s absence removes one of New England’s most productive young players from a rare Week 1 rematch of the previous season’s Super Bowl.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Plymouth volunteers help 94-year-old return to White Horse Beach
dek: Community members helped Alison Blomgren reach the sand after her daughter asked for assistance fulfilling a birthday wish.
body: A group of Plymouth volunteers helped a 94-year-old woman return to White Horse Beach after her daughter asked the community for assistance with a birthday wish.

NBC 10 WJAR reported that Alison Blomgren wanted to put her toes in the sand at the beach she remembered from childhood. Blomgren now lives in East Tennessee and has faced health and mobility challenges, making the trip onto the beach difficult.

Her daughter, Mari-Jane Shore, traveled with her to Massachusetts and sought help moving a wheelchair across the sand. Local residents responded, creating the support needed for Blomgren to reach the shoreline and spend time with family at the beach.

The visit followed the recent death of Blomgren’s husband and came around her September 4 birthday. The story is small compared with the day’s larger headlines, but it shows how a practical request can mobilize neighbors quickly. The volunteers’ assistance turned a place tied to childhood memory into an accessible birthday destination decades later.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Shaheen and Sullivan locked in close New Hampshire 1st District primary
dek: The Democratic contest for the open U.S. House seat remained uncalled late Tuesday, with two percentage points separating the candidates in an Associated Press tally.
body: Stefany Shaheen and Maura Sullivan remained locked in a close Democratic primary for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District late Tuesday, leaving one of the state’s most closely watched races without a declared winner.

NHPR reported that an Associated Press tally at 11 p.m. showed Shaheen with about 37% of the vote and Sullivan with about 35%, with roughly 70% counted. Those figures were preliminary, and the race had not been called.

The nomination is for the seat being vacated by U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, who won the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate earlier in the evening. The eventual Democratic nominee is set to face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo, whose primary victory was called Tuesday night.

The unresolved count is a material election-night development, not a forecast. Additional returns and any official canvassing will determine the final result. Voters should rely on updated results from election officials and established race-calling organizations rather than social-media claims while ballots continue to be reported.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Concord panel advances $22.4 million Memorial Field plan
dek: A joint city-school committee backed a two-phase renovation proposal, sending the project toward public hearings and votes by local governing bodies.
body: A joint Concord city-school committee has voted to advance a $22.4 million plan for renovating Memorial Field, moving the long-discussed project closer to public review and final decisions by the City Council and School Board.

The Concord Monitor reported that the committee approved the proposal, called “New Option A,” by a 3-1 vote. The plan is about $8.5 million less than an earlier concept and divides the work into two stages.

A first phase estimated at $13.9 million, including contingencies, would rebuild and expand the track, install an artificial-turf field, add roughly 1,000 to 1,500 bleacher seats and address drainage. A second phase, estimated at $8.5 million, would complete additional improvements.

The next steps are expected to include a public hearing, likely in October or November, followed by separate consideration from city and school officials. If financing and approvals line up, the first phase could take about two years. The phased approach gives Concord a way to address the field’s core athletic and infrastructure needs while leaving later work dependent on funding and future votes.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Nine charged in alleged Massachusetts benefit-fraud scheme
dek: Federal prosecutors say stolen identities were used to obtain nearly $1 million through SNAP, MassHealth and Social Security programs.
body: Nine people have been charged in an alleged fraud scheme involving nearly $1 million in public benefits, according to federal prosecutors cited by NBC 10 WJAR.

The government alleges that stolen identities were used to obtain identification documents and benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, MassHealth and Social Security. Prosecutors say some of the activity continued for extended periods, allowing benefits to accumulate under identities that did not belong to the defendants.

In one example described by the Justice Department, Mercedes Soto Capellan allegedly used a stolen identity to obtain approximately $65,521 in SNAP and MassHealth benefits. The broader total cited by authorities covers the alleged conduct of all nine defendants, not a single person.

The charges begin a court process and are not findings of guilt. Each defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. The case also highlights why benefit agencies cross-check identity, eligibility and payment records: fraud can divert limited program resources, but enforcement claims still must be tested through evidence and due process in court.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Angels end Red Sox five-game winning streak with 6-1 win
dek: Reid Detmers threw six scoreless innings and Zach Neto had four hits as Boston’s offense was held to four hits.
body: The Los Angeles Angels beat the Boston Red Sox 6-1 on Tuesday night, ending Boston’s five-game winning streak behind six scoreless innings from Reid Detmers and a four-hit performance by Zach Neto.

Detmers allowed one hit, struck out nine and walked one over 112 pitches. Neto went 4-for-5 and added a two-run homer in the ninth inning, his 24th of the season. Los Angeles finished with 15 hits after entering the game with only two victories in its previous 14 contests.

Boston managed four hits and struck out 13 times. Starter Patrick Sandoval allowed four runs on 10 hits over six innings. The Red Sox avoided a shutout in the seventh, when Nick Sogard delivered an RBI single.

The result tightened the focus on Boston’s offense after a productive winning stretch. It also gave the Angels their first victory over the Red Sox in five meetings this season. The score and statistics are the completed-game record reported after Tuesday’s final, not live market or in-game data.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Apple Cinemas plans multimillion-dollar Providence Place overhaul
dek: The theater operator says upgraded auditoriums, immersive screens and entertainment attractions are planned for the mall complex.
body: Apple Cinemas has announced a multimillion-dollar overhaul of its Providence Place theater, outlining new seating, projection and entertainment features for the downtown mall complex.

NBC 10 WJAR reported that every auditorium is slated to receive luxury recliners. The plan also calls for an ACX auditorium with Dolby Atmos sound and 4K projection, a SCREENX format that extends images onto side walls, and an existing IMAX auditorium upgraded to laser projection.

Beyond movies, the operator is planning immersive bowling and is considering interactive attractions built around archery, slingshot and drift-car experiences. Self-service beer and wine would be added only if the necessary approvals are obtained.

Apple Cinemas did not provide a completion date, so the announcement is best understood as a project plan rather than a finished renovation. If delivered, the changes would broaden the site from a conventional multiplex into a mixed entertainment venue. The timeline, final attraction list and any alcohol service remain subject to construction, permitting and other approvals.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Two face charges after Cranston traffic-stop drug seizure
dek: Police say a vehicle search produced about 30 grams of suspected methamphetamine, prescription pills and drug paraphernalia.
body: Two men face charges after a Cranston traffic stop led police to seize suspected methamphetamine, prescription pills and drug paraphernalia, according to the department’s account reported by NBC 10 WJAR.

Police said the stop occurred around 4:44 p.m. Monday on Wentworth Avenue. Officers allegedly saw drug paraphernalia in plain view and searched the vehicle, recovering about 30 grams of a substance that field-tested positive for methamphetamine, along with pills, a scale, a pipe and $90.

The driver was identified as Brandon Pierpont, 33, of Bellingham, Massachusetts, and the passenger as Miguel Rodriguez, 28, of Cranston. Police said both had active domestic-violence warrants. Pierpont also had a New Hampshire extradition warrant tied to narcotics charges.

Pierpont faces several drug-related counts, including possession with intent to deliver, while Rodriguez was charged with obstructing an officer and transferred to Woonsocket police. The allegations and field-test result will be subject to the court process; charges do not establish guilt, and laboratory testing may be used to confirm the substance.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Iran says it captured U.S. underwater drone near Strait of Hormuz
dek: The Pentagon confirmed a Dive-LD vehicle malfunctioned during a survey mission but said it carried no classified or sensitive equipment.
body: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that they captured a U.S. uncrewed underwater vehicle near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, adding another point of tension around the strategically important shipping passage.

Reuters reported that the Pentagon confirmed a Dive-LD drone had malfunctioned more than a day earlier during regional survey work. U.S. officials described it as an older version and said it carried no classified or sensitive equipment. Reuters said it could not independently verify Iran’s full account of the capture.

The roughly 19-foot autonomous vehicle was developed by Anduril for missions that can include seabed mapping, mine countermeasures and infrastructure inspection. Anduril confirmed the loss and said the system is intended for high-risk operations where equipment may not return.

The competing descriptions matter: Iran is presenting the episode as an intelligence and military gain, while the Pentagon is minimizing the sensitivity of the hardware. The incident remains developing because the vehicle’s exact condition, location and route to Iranian custody have not been independently established.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Relative says four family members found dead after Bahamas plane disappeared
dek: Relatives located the victims after launching a search for the small plane, which lost contact while flying toward Miami.
body: Four members of a family aboard a small plane that disappeared off the Bahamas were found dead Tuesday, a relative told The Associated Press.

Silvia Larrieu said relatives searching by boat recovered the bodies and were working with the U.S. Coast Guard to bring them home. The victims were Mario Lamar, 80; his wife, Lili Lamar, 79; and their grandchildren, Sofi Sosa, 28, and Christian Sosa, 22.

The PA-34 Piper left Great Harbour Cay in the Berry Islands on Monday morning for Miami Executive Airport. Bahamas police said air traffic control lost contact when the aircraft was about 13 miles west of Andros Island. Family members alerted authorities after messages went undelivered and the expected arrival time passed.

The Coast Guard sent an aircraft to assist after Bahamian authorities requested help, although poor weather delayed parts of the search. The developing work now centers on recovery and the investigation into what caused the plane to go down. Authorities had not announced a cause in the information available Tuesday night.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Cognition AI raises $2 billion at $48 billion valuation
dek: The autonomous coding-agent company says its run-rate revenue has climbed to nearly $900 million since a May financing.
body: AI coding startup Cognition AI said Tuesday that it raised $2 billion in a Series E financing that values the company at $48 billion, nearly double its valuation from a May funding round.

Reuters reported that new investors Andreessen Horowitz and Accel led the round, with Founders Fund, General Catalyst and Avenir also participating. Cognition said its run-rate revenue increased from $492 million to nearly $900 million since May, when it raised $1 billion at a $26 billion valuation.

The company builds autonomous software-engineering agents designed to plan, write, test and deploy code with limited human intervention. The fresh capital gives Cognition additional resources to develop those tools and compete in a crowded market for AI-assisted programming.

The $48 billion figure is a private financing valuation, not a continuously traded public-market price. It reflects the terms accepted by investors in this round and may not translate directly into a future sale or public listing value. Even so, the rapid step-up shows that large investors continue to place sizable bets on companies selling automation for software development.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Google redesigns European search results to comply with DMA
dek: The company is giving comparison services more prominence after an EU fine, while removing some real-time details from result carousels.
body: Google rolled out major changes to search results in Europe on Tuesday as it seeks to comply with the European Union’s Digital Markets Act and avoid additional penalties.

Reuters reported that the new layout gives more visibility to specialized comparison services for hotels, airlines, restaurants and other sectors. One service will appear prominently, followed by two others with fewer details, while business carousels will lose features including real-time prices. Google’s algorithm will determine the rankings.

The European Commission fined Google €460 million in July for favoring its own services and gave the company 60 days to comply or risk recurring penalties. The DMA is intended to limit the ability of large digital platforms to use their gatekeeper position to disadvantage rivals.

Google argues that the changes will reduce search quality and raise costs for European businesses. It also says earlier compliance changes cut free direct-booking traffic to European businesses by 30%. Those are company claims, not independent findings. Users outside the European Union are not affected by this rollout.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Adani Airports to raise about $1 billion from investor group
dek: The airport operator will issue new shares representing up to 5.54% to investors including Temasek, BlackRock, Premji Invest and Alpha Wave.
body: Adani Enterprises said its airport business will raise about $1 billion by issuing new shares to a group that includes Temasek, BlackRock-managed funds, Premji Invest and Alpha Wave.

Reuters reported that the investors will receive up to a 5.54% stake in Adani Airport Holdings. The transaction values the unit at roughly $18 billion before the new investment, while Adani Enterprises will remain the controlling shareholder.

The company plans to use the proceeds to expand and modernize its airport network, build airport-linked infrastructure and grow services such as ground handling and passenger operations. Adani Airport Holdings operates eight airports, including Mumbai International Airport, and accounts for about a quarter of India’s passenger traffic and one-third of its air cargo, according to the company.

The reported figures describe the announced financing terms, not a live share quote. For investors, the deal sets a fresh private valuation for the airport unit and brings outside capital into a business with large infrastructure needs. Completion and final ownership percentages remain subject to the transaction’s terms.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: LIV Golf files for Chapter 11 with more than $500 million in debt
dek: The league is seeking a court-supervised restructuring in New Jersey after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund ended financial support.
body: LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in New Jersey on Tuesday, listing more than $500 million in debt as it attempts to reorganize after losing its principal Saudi financial backing.

The Associated Press reported that the league listed estimated assets of $100 million to $500 million and liabilities of $500 million to $1 billion. Fourteen players were among its 30 largest creditors, with Jon Rahm listed as holding an unsecured claim of nearly $7.5 million.

LIV said BC Partners would be the primary source of capital under a restructuring plan. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, which ended regular support earlier this year, agreed to provide $49.6 million in debtor-in-possession financing, subject to court approval.

The proposed relaunch would use a smaller schedule, expand the field to 75 players and add a 54-hole cut and Monday qualifiers. LIV says it could emerge from bankruptcy and begin the new format as early as 2027. Chapter 11 generally allows a business to keep operating while it restructures, but the league’s future will depend on court approval, financing and which players remain.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: East Providence grower cultivates hundreds of pawpaw trees
dek: Joe Barros has spent 15 years building a backyard collection of North America’s largest native fruit and inviting neighbors to try it.
body: An East Providence backyard has become home to hundreds of pawpaw trees, part of resident Joe Barros’s effort to introduce more Rhode Islanders to a fruit that is native to North America but unfamiliar to many shoppers.

NBC 10 WJAR reported that Barros has grown the trees for 15 years. Pawpaws are considered North America’s largest native fruit, with a soft texture and tropical flavor. Barros describes the taste as a blend of mango and banana.

His interest began when tasting a pawpaw reminded him of childhood in Brazil. What started as curiosity developed into a large backyard collection and a personal campaign to share ripe fruit with visitors who have never encountered it.

Pawpaws can seem out of place in New England because of their tropical character, yet the species is native to the continent. Barros hopes wider interest could eventually make Rhode Island known for the fruit. For now, his garden is a local example of how one grower’s long-term experimentation can preserve an unusual crop and build community around harvest season.

author: NorthEast News Desk
headline: Aaron Judge returns to Yankees lineup after 84-game absence
dek: The New York captain started in right field Tuesday after recovering from a stress fracture in his right first rib.
body: Aaron Judge returned to the New York Yankees lineup Tuesday night after an 84-game absence, starting in right field and batting third against the Colorado Rockies.

The Yankees reinstated their captain from the 60-day injured list on Monday. Judge had not played since May 31 because of a stress fracture in his right first rib. The injury, which he believes occurred on a diving play in late April, was initially diagnosed as a bone bruise before later scans showed the fracture.

Judge resumed playing catch in mid-August after earlier running and light baseball work. He returned without a minor-league rehabilitation assignment. Before the injury, the three-time American League Most Valuable Player was batting .248 with 17 home runs and 38 RBIs in 59 games.

His return comes during a tight American League East race. Entering Tuesday, New York was 81-62, four games behind Tampa Bay and two ahead of Boston. Those standings are a dated pregame snapshot, not live results. The immediate question is how quickly Judge can regain game timing after missing most of the summer.

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: New Hampshire’s secretary of state has randomly selected ballot-counting devices from nine towns and city wards for post-election audits following Tuesday’s state primary.

The public checks are scheduled for Wednesday, September 9, at 10 a.m. and Thursday, September 10, at 9 a.m. at the New Hampshire State Archives in Concord. Members of the public and news media may observe the work.

Secretary of State David Scanlan’s office said one device will be audited from each selected location. The selections include communities using VotingWorks equipment and communities using Liberty Vote’s ImageCast Precinct 2 system, giving election officials samples from both voting technologies in use.

Officials must publish the audit findings by noon Friday, September 11. The process is separate from a candidate-requested recount: its purpose is to check how the selected devices recorded and counted ballots after Election Day. Results from the audit will provide a documented comparison for those locations while the state completes its post-primary election administration.
dek: Ballot-counting devices from nine towns and city wards will be checked publicly at the State Archives, with a report due Friday.
headline: New Hampshire selects nine locations for post-election audit
sourceName: New Hampshire Secretary of State via InDepthNH

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Chesterfield is considering temporary changes to police coverage after resignations left Chief Lance Rouse as the town department’s only employee legally able to answer calls.

Town Administrator Alissa Thompson said the community cannot expect one person to provide round-the-clock coverage. Local officials are weighing options that could reduce services or suspend full-time municipal policing while the town addresses staffing. The immediate challenge is maintaining emergency response without assuming the chief can be continuously available.

The staffing crisis unfolds alongside a lawsuit by former lieutenant John Ciarcia. He alleges that Rouse retaliated against him after he raised payroll questions. Rouse has also faced an accusation that he misled the New Hampshire Police Standards and Training Council. Those are allegations, and the cited report does not establish that they have been proven in court.

For residents, the practical issue is who will respond when the local department cannot. Town leaders have not announced a permanent arrangement. Any interim plan will need to clearly identify coverage, dispatch procedures and the role of neighboring or county law-enforcement agencies.
dek: A run of resignations has left Chief Lance Rouse as the only department employee legally able to respond, forcing the town to weigh temporary service changes.
headline: Chesterfield police chief becomes town’s only active officer

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Massachusetts began mailing its official voter-information guide Tuesday, giving residents eight weeks to review nine statewide ballot questions before the November general election.

Secretary of the Commonwealth William Galvin said the nine referendums tie the state record. The guide, commonly called the “Red Book,” is being sent to every household and summarizes each proposal along with arguments submitted by supporters and opponents.

The questions cover a wide range of state policy. Among them are proposals involving public-records rules for the Legislature and governor’s office, a conservation fund tied to sporting-goods tax revenue, and an all-candidate primary system. Voters will decide the measures separately from candidate contests on the same ballot.

The mailing starts an extended public-information period rather than signaling a position from election officials. Residents can use the guide to review the official wording and effects described for each question before voting. The unusually long ballot also gives local election departments another reason to urge voters to read the measures in advance rather than encountering them for the first time at a polling place.
dek: The state’s “Red Book” is headed to every household ahead of a general-election ballot containing a record-tying nine referendums.
headline: Massachusetts mails voter guide covering nine ballot questions

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Framingham man was held on $250,000 bail after his arraignment in connection with a Sunday-night crash that killed a pedestrian, according to local reports.

Authorities identified the defendant as 44-year-old Ronei DeOliveira and the victim as 62-year-old Philip Bligh. Police allege DeOliveira struck Bligh, left the scene on foot and later returned. Investigators said they detected signs of alcohol consumption.

DeOliveira faces charges including operating under the influence of alcohol, negligent operation and leaving the scene of a crash that caused death. The allegations have not been proven, and a criminal charge is not evidence of guilt.

The case remains in the early court process. The bail order determines the conditions for release while the prosecution continues; it is not a judgment on the charges. The incident adds urgency to police reminders that drivers involved in collisions must stop, seek emergency help and remain at the scene. Further details, including any additional evidence or court dates, will come through the Middlesex County proceedings.
dek: Prosecutors say a 44-year-old Framingham man struck and killed pedestrian Philip Bligh on Sunday night, left the scene and later returned.
headline: Driver held on $250,000 bail in fatal Framingham hit-and-run case

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Johnston’s school-bus contractor acknowledged a scheduling mistake Tuesday night as parents brought continuing complaints about late pickups, delayed drop-offs and long rides to the School Committee.

Zum said its route planning omitted 15 minutes needed to load elementary-school students. The company reported that on-time performance for some elementary drop-offs had fallen as low as 26 percent. It said it is reviewing route data and proposing adjustments, while also raising possible changes to school start and dismissal times.

Superintendent Scott Sutherland said legal questions around changing vendors would need to be discussed in executive session. The district began the school year with 10 bus monitors after a number of resignations and plans to add at least 13 more.

The meeting marks a concrete update after days of family complaints: the contractor identified a planning error and outlined potential responses, but the district has not announced a final remedy. Parents will be watching whether revised schedules reduce ride times and improve consistency without creating new disruptions for families. Any proposal to change school hours would require clear notice because it would affect transportation, childcare and work schedules across the community.
dek: Zum told the School Committee that its planning omitted 15 minutes for elementary-school loading as families pressed for fixes to late arrivals and long rides.
headline: Johnston school-bus contractor acknowledges scheduling error

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A discarded lithium-ion battery pack is believed to have started a fire inside a Waste Management trash truck in North Smithfield on Tuesday, local officials said.

The truck began smoking on Second Avenue. The driver moved it away from the residential area to a transfer station at 14 Canal Street, then emptied the burning load beside the road so firefighters could reach the material.

Crews extinguished the fire and used a thermal camera to identify a battery pack as the likely source. A Woonsocket hazardous-materials team contained and disposed of the battery, while Waste Management handled cleanup of the remaining debris. No injuries were reported.

The incident illustrates why rechargeable batteries should not go into household trash or curbside recycling. When crushed or punctured during collection and compaction, the cells can enter thermal runaway and ignite surrounding material. Residents should instead use a designated battery drop-off or household hazardous-waste program and cover exposed terminals when local guidance calls for it. The quick decision to move the truck away from homes limited the immediate risk, but the load still required specialized handling.
dek: Firefighters used a thermal camera to locate a lithium-ion battery after a Waste Management driver dumped the smoking load away from homes.
headline: Battery pack blamed for North Smithfield trash-truck fire

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Major British airports were working through a travel backlog early Wednesday after a technical failure in the United Kingdom’s air-traffic control system disrupted roughly 1,000 flights.

NATS, the country’s air-navigation service, said the fault affected flight-data processing and had been resolved. It said safety was not compromised. Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted were among the airports reporting delays or cancellations while airlines rebuilt schedules and repositioned aircraft and crews.

Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers were affected and that it canceled more than 50 flights. Those figures are the airline’s account of its own operation, while the broader effects varied by carrier and airport.

The technical fault is over, but the travel disruption remains a developing story because delays can carry into later departure waves even after air-traffic capacity returns. Passengers due to fly Wednesday should check directly with their airline before traveling and allow for changes to gates or departure times. Britain’s aviation regulator expects a full report on the incident, which will be central to understanding the cause and preventing a repeat.
dek: NATS said a flight-data processing fault was resolved, but cancellations and delays continued across major British airports as airlines repositioned aircraft and crews.
headline: UK airports work through backlog after air-traffic system failure

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: New flight-data evidence suggests the pilots of a cargo jet that crashed at Miami International Airport considered aborting the landing after touchdown, the National Transportation Safety Board said.

The Boeing 767, operated by 21 Air, overran the runway by about 1,300 feet Sunday and struck two vehicles, killing five people and injuring five. Investigators said the nose and right main landing gear touched down 30 seconds before the recording ended at about 158 knots; the main gear touched down 19 seconds before the end at about 134 knots.

The brakes were then released and the throttles advanced, movements consistent with an attempted go-around. The throttles returned to idle and braking resumed 11 seconds before the recording stopped. Investigators said the data showed no deployment of the speed brakes or thrust reversers.

The NTSB plans to interview the pilots Wednesday and release information from the cockpit voice recorder afterward. The findings are preliminary and do not establish a cause. One runway has reopened, but investigators still need to reconcile the aircraft data, crew actions, runway conditions and physical evidence before reaching conclusions.
dek: Investigators say throttle and brake movements suggest the pilots briefly tried a go-around after touchdown before the Boeing 767 overran the runway.
headline: NTSB data indicates Miami cargo crew considered aborting landing

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Australia’s government has proposed legislation that would require social-media platforms to let users age 16 and older opt out of algorithmically recommended feeds.

Under the plan, services would have to notify eligible users and provide a genuine, enduring choice between recommendation-driven content and a feed centered on friends or creators they follow. The proposal extends Australia’s scrutiny of platform design beyond its existing ban on social-media accounts for children under 16.

A broader digital duty of care would also apply to services including games, apps and artificial-intelligence chatbots. Those companies would be expected to protect children from features regulators consider addictive or damaging to self-esteem. The maximum penalty described for a breach is 109.2 million Australian dollars, equivalent to about $78.6 million in the Associated Press report.

The measures are proposed laws and have not yet taken effect. Their practical impact will depend on the final text, parliamentary approval and enforcement rules. If enacted, the opt-out requirement could test whether large platforms can provide a truly persistent non-algorithmic experience rather than a temporary setting that quietly resets.
dek: Draft legislation would require social platforms to give users 16 and older a lasting choice between recommended content and posts from accounts they follow.
headline: Australia proposes right to opt out of algorithmic feeds

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Jury selection began Tuesday in New York in the federal racketeering trial of Huawei, opening a closely watched case over the Chinese telecommunications company’s global business practices.

An indictment accuses Huawei of participating in a long-running scheme involving trade-secret and technology theft, wire and bank fraud, and business in North Korea despite U.S. sanctions. Prosecutors also allege the company supplied surveillance equipment that helped Iranian authorities monitor protesters in 2009.

Huawei denies the accusations. Its lawyers have argued that the government’s claims are vague and overreaching and have called the prosecution’s broader narrative demonstrably false. The charges are allegations, and the company is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Opening statements were expected no earlier than Wednesday after a jury is seated. The trial could bring new testimony and documents into public view about Huawei’s expansion, which now includes advanced chips as well as network equipment and consumer devices. The company has been barred from selling equipment to U.S. wireless carriers, but the criminal case will be decided on the evidence presented in court, not those separate regulatory restrictions.
dek: Federal prosecutors accuse the telecommunications company of a long-running scheme involving trade secrets, fraud and sanctions violations; Huawei denies the allegations.
headline: Huawei racketeering trial begins with jury selection in New York

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Oil prices climbed toward $100 a barrel in early Asian trading Wednesday as investors continued to assess risks to energy supplies, while regional equity markets opened mixed.

At 2:27 a.m. UTC, Reuters reported Brent crude up $1.57 at $99.49 a barrel, its highest level since late June. U.S. West Texas Intermediate was up $1.60 at $94.63. Both were heading for a fourth consecutive session of gains. These are timestamped market snapshots, not live prices.

Equities did not move in one direction. Australia’s benchmark was down 0.3 percent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 0.6 percent and China’s CSI 300 added 0.2 percent. Japan’s Nikkei gained 0.6 percent, South Korea’s Kospi rose 1.6 percent and Taiwan’s market added 0.6 percent.

Currency markets also reflected caution: the yen traded near a seven-month high, while the euro edged higher before a European Central Bank decision. For Northeast households and businesses, a sustained oil move can eventually affect heating fuel, transportation and shipping costs, but the early-session price alone does not determine retail prices.
dek: Brent reached its highest level since late June in early Wednesday trading while regional stock indexes split between gains and losses.
headline: Oil approaches $100 as Asian markets open mixed

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Shares of Indian technology-services firm Coforge fell more than 7 percent Wednesday after chairman Om Prakash Bhatt resigned following concerns tied to the company’s board-evaluation process.

At 9:16 a.m. India Standard Time, the stock was down 7.12 percent at 1,809.20 rupees, according to Reuters. That figure is a dated early-session snapshot, not a live quote, and the price may move as trading continues.

Bhatt’s departure followed concerns identified through an internal audit of how the board evaluation was conducted. Investors often treat unexpected board-level resignations as a governance risk because they can create uncertainty about oversight, controls and future disclosures, even before the underlying issue is fully explained.

The next material information will come from Coforge’s formal filings and any account of corrective steps. A one-day price move does not by itself establish the long-term effect on operations or financial performance. For now, the decline reflects an immediate market reaction to leadership and process concerns at a company serving global clients in software and information-technology services.
dek: The Indian IT-services company dropped more than 7 percent after Om Prakash Bhatt left following concerns identified in an internal audit.
headline: Coforge shares fall after chairman resigns over board-review concerns

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Two American flags inside Boston Logan International Airport have marked the departure points of American Airlines Flight 11 and United Airlines Flight 175 for nearly 25 years.

The planes left Logan on September 11, 2001, and were hijacked before striking the World Trade Center. Airport workers placed the flags near the associated gates in the weeks after the attacks, creating a simple memorial visible to passengers and crews. The flags face the taxiways and have remained part of the terminal landscape through renovations and the passage of time.

The tribute complements the airport’s public 9/11 Memorial, which honors the passengers and crews aboard both flights. Together, the sites connect a national tragedy to the specific place where those journeys began.

As the 25th anniversary approaches, the flags carry a different kind of weight for travelers who were born after the attacks as well as for workers who remember that morning. They do not interrupt airport operations or require a ceremony to be noticed. Their permanence is the point: a quiet, daily acknowledgement embedded in one of New England’s busiest public spaces.
dek: For 25 years, American flags near the gates used by Flights 11 and 175 have honored the passengers and crews who departed Boston on September 11, 2001.
headline: Logan Airport’s two 9/11 flags maintain a quiet memorial

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Before “9 to 5” became a hit song and movie, it was the name of a Boston organizing effort led by women office workers seeking fairer treatment on the job.

The movement began in the early 1970s among secretaries and clerical workers who compared experiences with low wages, limited advancement and sexual harassment. By organizing around shared workplace problems, 9to5 helped make issues that were often treated as private frustrations part of a public labor agenda.

Its influence reached popular culture through the 1980 film starring Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Dolly Parton and Parton’s title song. The comedy gave a broad audience a recognizable picture of office hierarchies and the frustrations that had motivated the original organizers.

The Boston roots matter because they show how a local worker network can shape a national conversation. Decades later, arguments over pay transparency, harassment protections and advancement still echo the movement’s early demands. The anniversary coverage is also a reminder that the familiar phrase “9 to 5” carries two histories: one in entertainment and another in organized workplace advocacy.
dek: A campaign organized by women office workers in the early 1970s pushed for fair pay and an end to workplace harassment, later inspiring a film and Dolly Parton anthem.
headline: Boston-born 9to5 movement’s labor legacy returns to focus

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Stefany Shaheen won the Democratic primary in New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District after a close contest with former Navy official Maura Sullivan, according to results reported by NHPR.

The result advances Shaheen, a former Portsmouth city councilor, to the general election for the open U.S. House seat. She will face Anthony DiLorenzo, who won the Republican primary. The district includes Manchester, the Seacoast and communities across southeastern New Hampshire.

The Democratic race remained uncalled late Tuesday as election officials continued reporting results. Shaheen’s victory is the meaningful update: the uncertainty described earlier in the evening has been resolved, setting the matchup for November.

The contest will determine who succeeds the district’s current representative. Both campaigns now move from intraparty competition to a general-election electorate, while state officials complete routine canvassing and certification work. This report does not project the November result; it reflects the primary outcome reported after additional returns were counted.
dek: The former Portsmouth city councilor prevailed over Maura Sullivan and will face Republican Anthony DiLorenzo for the open U.S. House seat.
headline: Stefany Shaheen wins narrow Democratic primary in New Hampshire’s 1st District

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Nearly 300 people in New Hampshire may lose full Medicaid coverage on October 1 as new federal eligibility limits take effect, according to state figures reported by NHPR.

The Department of Health and Human Services identified 296 residents who could be affected. Under the change, adults who are not pregnant generally must be a U.S. citizen or national, a lawful permanent resident, a Cuban-Haitian Entrant or a migrant covered by the Compacts of Free Association to keep full Medicaid eligibility.

Eligibility rules are not changing for people younger than 19, pregnant patients or women during the year after pregnancy. Some residents who lose full benefits may still qualify for emergency Medicaid, and others may be able to seek coverage through the insurance marketplace.

The change is especially consequential for people receiving ongoing or long-term care. State officials said they contacted everyone identified as potentially affected, though one family profiled by NHPR disputed receiving notice. Residents who believe their status is incorrect can contact the state or a benefits counselor before coverage changes.
dek: State health officials identified 296 people whose full coverage may end when federal eligibility rules narrow for some noncitizens.
headline: Nearly 300 New Hampshire residents may lose Medicaid October 1

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A 21-year-old New Bedford man died from injuries sustained in a motorcycle crash at Walnut and South Sixth streets, police said.

Officers responded at about 9:55 p.m. Friday and found a heavily damaged motorcycle and a Saturn sedan at the intersection. The motorcyclist, identified as Anthony Navarro Rodriguez, was taken first to a local hospital and then airlifted for additional treatment. Police said he was pronounced dead Saturday.

The person driving the Saturn remained at the scene and cooperated with investigators, according to police. Authorities have not announced charges or released a preliminary determination about what caused the collision.

The crash remains under investigation. Police have not publicly identified the sedan driver or provided additional information about road conditions, speed or other possible factors. Those details should not be inferred while investigators continue collecting evidence. Anyone with information about the collision can contact New Bedford police through the department’s regular reporting channels.
dek: Police say 21-year-old Anthony Navarro Rodriguez died after a Friday night collision with a sedan; the investigation remains open.
headline: New Bedford motorcyclist dies after Walnut Street crash

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Two drivers were seriously injured when a motorcycle and an SUV collided on Route 18 in Lakeville, police said.

The crash was reported at about 6:24 p.m. Monday and involved a Yamaha motorcycle and a Honda CR-V. Police said the man riding the motorcycle and the woman driving the SUV were both taken to Morton Hospital with serious injuries. Neither vehicle was carrying a passenger.

Route 18 was closed while emergency crews treated the drivers and investigators documented the scene. The closure was part of the immediate response; officials did not say the road remained closed after the investigation at the scene was completed.

Authorities have not released the names or ages of the drivers, an update on their conditions, or a preliminary cause. The investigation is continuing, and police have not announced citations or charges. Drivers with relevant dash-camera footage or firsthand information can contact Lakeville police. Until investigators release additional findings, it is not clear how the vehicles came into contact.
dek: A Yamaha motorcycle and Honda CR-V collided on Route 18 Monday evening, sending both drivers to Morton Hospital.
headline: Motorcycle-SUV crash seriously injures two in Lakeville

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Two Massachusetts men face larceny charges in separate cases involving casino cheques at Bally’s Twin River in Lincoln, Rhode Island State Police said.

In the first case, police allege Arturo Ramos of Sharon took two purple gaming cheques, each valued at $500, on August 17. Investigators said casino security video, player-club information and vehicle records helped identify him. Police said Ramos later surrendered and returned the cheques.

In the second case, authorities allege Kaheem Campbell of Amherst picked up an orange cheque that another patron dropped on July 18. Police said casino records and a driver’s-license photograph were used during the investigation, and Campbell was arrested at the casino on August 20.

Both men were charged with larceny under $1,500. The incidents are unrelated, and the charges are allegations that must be proved in court. Officials did not announce final case dispositions. Neither arrest establishes guilt, and each defendant is presumed innocent unless convicted.
dek: Rhode Island State Police say unrelated incidents involved gaming cheques picked up from casino tables or floors; both cases are allegations.
headline: Two men charged in separate Twin River casino cheque thefts

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A family escaped safely after smoke alarms alerted them to an early-morning fire at a home on Brayton Avenue in Cranston, officials said.

Firefighters were called at about 3:30 a.m. Tuesday to the property near Rock Hill Drive. Investigators believe the fire started outside the house and then spread into the building. Crews brought the flames under control, and no injuries were reported.

Officials credited the working alarms with giving the occupants time to leave before conditions worsened. Authorities did not immediately identify a specific ignition source or release an estimate of the damage.

The investigation remains open. The response also underscores the role of working smoke alarms in detecting a fire before sleeping residents see or smell danger. Fire-safety agencies generally advise testing alarms regularly and replacing units according to manufacturer guidance, but officials did not connect any broader warning to this specific incident. The immediate finding was straightforward: everyone inside got out safely.
dek: Fire officials believe flames began outside a Brayton Avenue home before spreading inside; everyone escaped without injury.
headline: Smoke alarms help Cranston family escape early-morning fire

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Russian drones struck a crossing on the Ukraine-Moldova border overnight, causing deaths, injuries and fires, Ukraine’s border guard service said early Wednesday.

Officials had not provided a precise casualty count in the initial report carried by Reuters. The limited information makes the scale of the attack unclear, and emergency crews were still responding at the time of the first public statements.

Kyiv also came under attack overnight. Ukraine’s emergency service reported fires in the capital but said no casualties had been recorded there in the initial assessment. The two locations were part of a broader overnight threat, though officials had not released a complete accounting of launches, interceptions or damage.

This is a developing story because casualty figures and site conditions may change as local authorities complete searches and damage assessments. Early wartime claims can also be revised. The confirmed core facts at publication are that Ukraine reported a Russian drone strike at the border crossing, acknowledged casualties without an exact number, and separately reported fires in Kyiv.
dek: Ukraine’s border service reported deaths, injuries and fires after an overnight strike, while Kyiv also faced attacks without reported casualties.
headline: Russian drones hit Ukraine-Moldova border crossing

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: The U.S. Treasury Department imposed 36 new Iran-related sanctions Tuesday, with most of the designations focused on aviation companies and their support networks, Reuters reported.

The action targeted 27 Iranian airlines and related businesses, along with front companies, cargo handlers and intermediaries in Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Malaysia and Kazakhstan. Treasury also suspended aviation authorizations that had allowed certain overflights and some commercial aircraft operations.

The measures expand financial and operational pressure on Iran’s aviation sector, including Mahan Air. A designation generally blocks property subject to U.S. jurisdiction and restricts transactions by U.S. persons, but the practical effect on individual flights and carriers will depend on implementation and compliance outside the United States.

The sanctions are part of a developing U.S. policy response and are distinct from recent military events in the region. Treasury published the designations through its Office of Foreign Assets Control. Additional guidance or licensing decisions could clarify the scope, so this report reflects the agency action announced Tuesday rather than predicting its longer-term impact.
dek: The Treasury Department designated dozens of airlines and related entities while suspending authorizations for some Iranian aviation activity.
headline: U.S. expands Iran aviation sanctions in new Treasury action

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Dutch payments company Adyen plans to expand further in India after sharply increasing its local workforce and securing licenses needed to process domestic and cross-border transactions.

The company had about 120 employees in India during the first half of 2026, ten times its 2023 headcount, Reuters reported. Adyen received payment-aggregator and cross-border licenses in 2024 and says it plans more hiring, though it did not give a target.

Adyen is modifying its platform for India-specific requirements, including data localization, recurring-payment mandates and the Unified Payments Interface. Its Indian business reported pretax income of 3.18 million euros in 2025, up from 1.45 million euros a year earlier.

The expansion places Adyen in a large but tightly regulated digital-payments market. The company is also preparing for so-called agentic commerce, in which software agents help initiate purchases, but adoption and regulation are still evolving. The figures describe completed reporting periods and announced plans; they are not a live measure of revenue, transaction volume or valuation.
dek: The Dutch payments company has increased its India workforce tenfold since 2023 and is adapting its platform to local payment rules.
headline: Adyen plans further India expansion as local business grows

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Flashlight Capital Partners has requested shareholder registers from five Samsung companies as the activist investor presses for changes at South Korean security-services provider S-1.

The five affiliates together hold 20.6% of S-1, according to Reuters. Flashlight began its campaign in June and disclosed a position valued at about $40 million, equivalent to roughly 2% of the company’s market capitalization at the time.

Last month, Flashlight offered to buy all S-1 shares held by the five Samsung units for 906.6 billion won, or about $676 million. The proposed 116,000 won per-share price represented a 45.2% premium to S-1’s August 26 closing price. Japanese security company SECOM remains S-1’s largest shareholder with a 25.7% stake, while S-1 holds about 11% of its own shares.

Samsung affiliates declined to comment, and S-1 said it had no position on the request. S-1 shares opened Wednesday at 78,900 won, down 0.4%; that figure is a timestamped market move, not a live quote.
dek: Flashlight Capital Partners wants records from five Samsung affiliates that together own 20.6% of the security-services company.
headline: Activist investor seeks Samsung shareholder registers in S-1 campaign

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: India’s National Stock Exchange is likely to price its initial public offering between 1,700 and 1,785 rupees per share, according to a source familiar with the plans cited by Reuters.

At the top of that expected range, the exchange would be valued at roughly 4.4 trillion rupees, or $46.4 billion. The listing is targeted for the week of September 21 and would rank among India’s largest stock-market debuts.

NSE is the dominant venue for Indian equity derivatives and the world’s most active derivatives exchange when measured by contract volume. That scale makes the offering important beyond the amount raised: public-market investors would gain direct exposure to trading, clearing and market-data revenue tied to India’s expanding capital markets.

The proposed range has not yet become a final offer price, and terms can change before books close. The valuation figures are based on the reported range and exchange rates at publication. They should not be read as a live market price or as a prediction of how the shares will trade after listing.
dek: The expected range could value the exchange at about $46.4 billion at the top end ahead of a planned September listing.
headline: NSE India IPO likely to target 1,700 to 1,785 rupees a share

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Confidence among major Japanese manufacturers rose to its strongest level in nearly five years in September, supported by demand for semiconductors and data-center equipment.

The Reuters Tankan manufacturing index increased to plus 21 from plus 18 in August, its highest reading since December 2021. Electronics manufacturers recorded a particularly strong improvement, climbing to plus 39 from plus 24. A positive reading means optimists outnumber pessimists.

Sentiment among nonmanufacturers also improved, reaching plus 29 from plus 28. Looking three months ahead, manufacturers expected their index to rise further to plus 27, while service-sector respondents anticipated a slight easing to plus 27.

The survey was conducted from August 26 through September 4 and received responses from 224 of 510 companies. Businesses still cited risks including Middle East tensions, higher raw-material costs and softer consumer spending. The results are a survey of corporate sentiment, not a direct measure of current production or stock prices, but they provide an early view of business conditions before official data.
dek: A Reuters survey showed electronics demand lifting factory confidence, while services sentiment also edged higher.
headline: Japan manufacturer sentiment reaches nearly five-year high

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Retired NASA astronaut Barry “Butch” Wilmore visited two Warwick schools Tuesday, giving Rhode Island students a firsthand account of life and work in space.

Wilmore spoke at Winman Middle School and Scott Elementary School. The retired U.S. Navy captain spent a combined 464 days in space over three missions, experience that gave students a direct connection to human spaceflight beyond textbooks and video.

Warwick Mayor Frank Picozzi welcomed Wilmore, and former local broadcaster John Loughlin helped arrange the visit, according to NBC 10 WJAR. Photos from the schools showed students gathered for the presentations and meeting the astronaut.

The visit came after Wilmore’s retirement from NASA and focused on education rather than a new mission announcement. For students, the value was the chance to ask questions of someone who has flown multiple spacecraft and lived for extended periods in orbit. School officials did not announce a continuing program tied to the appearance, making Tuesday’s sessions a special one-day event.
dek: The retired NASA astronaut and Navy captain visited Winman Middle School and Scott Elementary after completing 464 days in space.
headline: Astronaut Butch Wilmore brings space stories to Warwick schools

author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Campanella’s in Cranston is scheduled to reopen September 16, bringing the longtime restaurant back after a closure tied to court-supervised receivership proceedings.

The Campanella family purchased the restaurant from a court-appointed receiver several months ago and is preparing the dining room and kitchen for a grand reopening. The return restores a familiar local name and puts the business back under family ownership.
